The consumables in a tool kit are as decisive as the tools, and choosing the wrong chemistry is the commonest reason a repair fails a fortnight later.

Adhesives divide by what they bond and how they cure. Polyvinyl acetate, ordinary white wood glue, bonds timber by penetrating the fibres and, in a well-fitted joint, produces a bond stronger than the wood itself; it needs clamping for around thirty minutes and full strength takes 24 hours, and the exterior grades are labelled D3 or D4. Cyanoacrylate, superglue, cures in seconds by reacting with surface moisture, works best on close-fitting rigid surfaces, and is brittle under impact. Two-part epoxy mixes a resin and a hardener and gives the strongest gap-filling bond across dissimilar materials such as metal to ceramic, with working times from five minutes to an hour. Polyurethane construction adhesive foams slightly as it cures, filling gaps and bonding almost anything, and it is what holds a loose stair tread or a panel to masonry. Contact adhesive is applied to both surfaces, left until touch-dry, and grabs on contact, which means no repositioning is possible.

Sealants are different from adhesives, being designed to stay flexible and exclude water. Silicone is the correct choice around baths, showers and sinks, and the sanitary or mould-resistant grades contain a fungicide; it cannot be painted. Acrylic frame sealant, sometimes called decorator's caulk, fills gaps between skirting, architrave and wall, and can be painted, but it is not waterproof and will fail in a shower. Expanding polyurethane foam fills large voids and must be used sparingly, since it can expand with enough force to bow a door frame.

Tapes are frequently misused. PTFE tape seals plumbing threads. Electrical insulating tape is rated for voltage and temperature and should not be used as a mechanical repair. Duct tape has a fabric scrim and strong adhesive but degrades with heat and time, leaving a residue, and it is genuinely poor at sealing heating ducts. Self-amalgamating tape fuses to itself into a solid rubber sleeve and is excellent for temporary pipe and cable repairs. Masking tape protects surfaces during painting and should be removed while the paint is still slightly soft.

Lubricants deserve one clarification, because the common aerosol penetrating spray is a water-displacing penetrant, not a long-term lubricant, and it washes away existing grease. Use it to free seized parts, then apply the right lubricant afterwards: light machine oil for hinges and mechanisms, white lithium grease for metal-on-metal loads, silicone spray for rubber, plastic and window channels, and dry graphite or PTFE powder for locks, since oil in a lock attracts dust and eventually gums the mechanism solid.

sections.heading: Protective Equipment
sections.body:
Protective equipment is the cheapest insurance in the kit and the item most often skipped, usually on the reasoning that the job is small. The injury statistics point the other way: the majority of domestic tool injuries occur during brief, routine tasks by people who did not consider them hazardous.

Eye protection is the non-negotiable item. The eye has no meaningful defence against a fragment travelling at speed, blinking is far too slow, and the damage is frequently permanent. Impact-rated safety glasses conforming to EN 166 or ANSI Z87.1 cost very little; ordinary spectacles are not eye protection, since their lenses are not impact-rated and their frames offer no lateral coverage. Wear them for all striking, cutting, drilling, grinding and anything overhead, and for handling chemicals, where goggles that seal against the face are better than glasses. Grinding and using an angle grinder demand a full face shield over safety glasses, because grinding discs can burst.

Hearing protection matters because damage is cumulative, painless and irreversible. Sound levels are measured in decibels on the A-weighted scale, and the exposure limit halves for every three-decibel increase. Eighty-five decibels is roughly the threshold for concern over a working day; a circular saw or angle grinder runs around 100 to 110 decibels, at which safe exposure drops to a few minutes. Foam plugs correctly inserted give around 25 to 30 decibels of attenuation and cost almost nothing; earmuffs are easier to put on and take off repeatedly.

Respiratory protection is where household work most often goes wrong, because dust looks harmless. Silica dust from cutting or drilling concrete, brick and tile causes silicosis and lung cancer, and the exposure from a few minutes of dry cutting can be substantial. Wood dust, particularly from hardwoods and manufactured boards containing formaldehyde resins, is a recognised carcinogen. A disposable FFP2 mask, roughly equivalent to the American N95, is the sensible minimum for dusty work, with FFP3 for silica; both require a seal against clean-shaven skin, and a beard defeats them. Better still, control dust at source with on-tool extraction or by wetting the material.

Hands and feet complete the set. Cut-resistant gloves suit handling sheet metal and glass, general-purpose grip gloves suit rough materials, and nitrile gloves suit chemicals; the important exception is that gloves must not be worn near rotating machinery, where they can catch and pull a hand in. Sturdy closed shoes, ideally with a toe cap, prevent the dropped-tool injury that is otherwise a near-certainty over a lifetime of small jobs.

Finally, keep a stocked first aid kit within reach and know where it is before you need it. Blue-coloured plasters are the catering convention because they are visible if they come off in food, and the same logic makes them easy to spot in a work area.

sections.heading: Buying the Kit in Stages
sections.body:
Buying everything at once is expensive and produces a box full of tools you never use. The rational approach is three tiers, purchased as need and budget allow, with each tier fully useful on its own. Large pre-packed sets are generally poor value: they pad the item count with low-quality small pieces and rarely include the two or three tools that actually matter.

Tier one covers the tasks that recur in every household: assembling furniture, hanging pictures, tightening what has worked loose, and dealing with an immediate emergency. Tier two adds the cordless drill and the tools that make larger jobs practical. Tier three covers occasional and specialised work and is often better hired than bought, since tool hire is inexpensive for a one-day job and avoids storing something used twice a decade.

A word on where to buy. Independent trade suppliers and builders' merchants generally sell better tools at lower prices than general retailers, and their staff can tell you which fixing suits your wall. Second-hand hand tools, particularly older hammers, chisels, planes and spanners, are frequently superior to new budget equivalents, since the steel in mid-twentieth-century tools was often excellent and wear is visible. This does not extend to anything with a safety function: never buy second-hand voltage testers, protective equipment, ladders or power tools of unknown history.
ingredients: Tier one, the essential core: a 450 gram claw hammer; a set of quality screwdrivers covering slotted, Phillips and Pozidriv; a magnetic bit driver with a bit set; combination pliers and long-nose pliers; a 250 millimetre adjustable wrench; a 5 metre tape measure; a small combination square; a 600 millimetre spirit level; a retractable utility knife with spare blades; a hex key set in metric and imperial; a torch; and impact-rated safety glasses.

Tier one consumables: an assortment of woodscrews in common sizes; wall plugs matched to your wall type; picture hooks; PTFE tape; insulating tape; white wood glue; superglue; a penetrating and water-displacing spray; and a mixed pack of batteries.

Tier two, the capability step: an 18 volt cordless combi drill with two batteries; a set of twist, masonry and brad-point drill bits; a stud and cable detector; a hardpoint handsaw and a hacksaw; water-pump pliers; locking pliers; a socket set from 8 to 19 millimetres; two G-clamps or quick-release clamps; a small pry bar; a nail punch; a soft-faced mallet; a two-pole voltage indicator; insulated screwdrivers; wire strippers; and a caulking gun.

Tier two consumables: silicone sanitary sealant; acrylic decorator's caulk; two-part epoxy; construction adhesive; sandpaper in coarse, medium and fine grades; filler; and dust masks rated FFP2 or FFP3.

Tier three, occasional and specialised: a multimeter; a basin wrench and a pipe cutter; a plunger and a drain auger; a laser level; a digital caliper; a wood chisel set; a hand plane; a heat gun; a step ladder rated to your weight; and a wet-and-dry vacuum.

Better hired than bought for most households: an SDS rotary hammer drill; an angle grinder; a circular saw; a wallpaper steamer; a floor sander; a carpet stretcher; scaffold towers; and a pipe freezing kit.

sections.heading: Storage, Organisation and Maintenance
sections.body:
A tool you cannot find is a tool you do not own, and the time lost searching is the reason many small repairs never happen. Organisation is therefore part of the kit rather than an afterthought.

The first principle is a defined home for every tool, so that its absence is visible. A shadow board, with outlines drawn around each hanging tool, achieves this instantly and is why professional workshops use them. In a toolbox, the equivalent is foam or moulded trays. The second principle is separation by use, so that the tools for the commonest jobs live together and can be carried in one trip. A cantilever toolbox or a tool bag holding the tier-one set, kept somewhere accessible in the house rather than in a distant shed or garage, means small jobs get done rather than postponed.

Storage conditions determine tool life. The enemy is moisture, because steel corrodes rapidly at relative humidity above about 60 per cent, and unheated garages and sheds swing through the dew point daily, condensing water on cold metal. Keep tools indoors where possible; where that is impossible, a sealed container with silica gel or a low-power dehumidifier makes a substantial difference. A light wipe of oil on bare steel, or a spray of a water-displacing product, prevents surface rust. Lithium-ion batteries should be stored around 40 to 60 per cent charged, away from freezing and away from heat, and never left permanently on a charger that lacks maintenance mode.

Maintenance is mostly a matter of small, regular attention. Wipe tools clean before putting them away, since plaster, adhesive and salt from hands all promote corrosion. Check hammer heads and axe heads for tightness. Replace utility knife blades often. Keep saw teeth from contacting other metal, ideally with a blade guard. Oil pivots on pliers and adjustable wrenches. Sharpen chisels and plane irons on a stone as soon as they stop cutting cleanly rather than persisting with a blunt edge, which is both harder work and more dangerous.

Surface rust that has already formed is usually recoverable. Fine abrasive paper of around 400 grit with a little oil, or a soaked cloth of white vinegar for pitted areas followed by neutralising with bicarbonate of soda solution and thorough drying, restores most tools. Deep pitting on a cutting edge is generally terminal.

Finally, keep the consumables inventoried in a way you will actually maintain. A shallow compartment box of screws, plugs and picture hooks, with the sizes labelled, converts a trip to a shop into a two-minute job, and that difference is what decides whether a repair happens at all. Buying screws and plugs in bulk boxes rather than small packets costs a fraction as much per item and means you are never short by two.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Knowing When to Stop
sections.body:
A predictable set of errors accounts for most damaged work, damaged tools and injuries in domestic repair, and nearly all of them are errors of substitution or of pressing on.

Substitution is the first family. Using a screwdriver as a chisel or a pry bar bends the shaft and can snap the tip, sending hardened steel across the room. Using pliers on a nut rounds the corners and makes the fastener far harder to remove afterwards. Using a chrome socket on an impact driver risks fracture. Using a wood bit in masonry, or a masonry bit in tile, destroys both bit and workpiece. The general rule is that a tool used outside its design purpose fails in a way that is sudden rather than gradual, which is why substitution is disproportionately associated with injury.

Force is the second family. When a fastener will not move, the instinct is to apply more torque, which usually rounds the head and converts an inconvenience into an extraction job. The better sequence is to stop, seat the tool fully, apply penetrating oil and wait ten minutes, try shock rather than steady force by tapping the tool, use a longer lever or a breaker bar, and only then consider heat or a screw extractor. Similarly, a screw that suddenly spins freely has stripped its hole or fixing, and driving it harder achieves nothing; the repairs are a larger fixing, a plug of glued dowel or matchsticks in the hole, or moving the position.

Preparation errors are the third family. Measuring once. Failing to check for cables and pipes before drilling, which causes the most dangerous common domestic accident. Not isolating water or power. Not clamping the workpiece. Not reading the fixing packet for the specified drill diameter. Each of these takes under a minute and each prevents a disproportionate amount of damage.

Knowing when to stop is a skill in itself, and there are clear thresholds. Stop and call a professional for anything involving gas, which in most jurisdictions is legally restricted and where an error kills by explosion or carbon monoxide poisoning. Stop for structural work, meaning removing or notching a wall, beam or joist, since the load path may not be what it appears. Stop for consumer units, new circuits and anything electrical beyond your legal scope. Stop for suspected asbestos in any building predating about 1980, which should be tested rather than disturbed. Stop for work at height beyond a short step ladder. Stop when you have taken something apart and no longer understand how it goes back, before removing anything further, and photograph each stage next time.

The final honest test is whether you can explain what will happen if the repair fails. If the answer is a small mess, proceed. If it is a flood, a fire, a shock or a collapse, get help.

guides.safetyNote: Isolate electrical circuits at the consumer unit and prove them dead with a tested voltage indicator before touching any wiring; in many jurisdictions certain electrical and all gas work is legally restricted to registered trades. Buildings from before about 1980 may contain asbestos and those from before about 1978 may contain lead paint, neither of which should be sanded, drilled or broken up without testing and proper controls. Wear eye protection for any cutting, striking, drilling or grinding, and stop and call a professional when structure, gas, water under pressure or mains electricity are involved and you are unsure.

guides.title: Hand Saws and How to Cut Straight
guides.summary: How a saw tooth actually severs wood, what separates rip from crosscut filing, how to choose among panel saws, backsaws, Japanese pull saws and the specialist patterns, and the marking, stance and stroke that produce a straight square cut, together with sharpening and the diagnosis of every common way a cut goes wrong.

sections.heading: Why the Hand Saw Still Earns Its Place
sections.body:
A hand saw is a strip of hardened steel with teeth filed along one edge, and it is among the oldest tools still in daily use, with copper-toothed examples surviving from Egypt around 3000 BCE. Power tools have not made it obsolete, and the reasons are practical rather than sentimental. A hand saw needs no electricity, makes no dust cloud, cannot kick a board back at you, costs a fraction of a table saw, occupies the space of a shelf, and can be brought to work that cannot be brought to a machine, such as a joist in a loft or a door hung in its frame. For a single cut, a hand saw is usually faster than setting up a machine to make it.

There is also a control argument. A hand saw cuts at perhaps one or two strokes a second, which means a wandering cut can be seen and corrected while it happens. A circular saw makes the same error in a tenth of a second and there is nothing to be done afterwards. For joinery in particular, the fine backsaws used to cut dovetails and tenons remain the standard tool because they are steerable, and because a skilled sawyer can split a pencil line more reliably than most jigs can be set.

The reputation hand saws have for being difficult is largely the fault of the saws most people have met. The hardpoint saws sold in builders' merchants have induction-hardened teeth, glassy and grey rather than bright, which cut aggressively when new and cannot be sharpened when blunt, so they are thrown away. Most people's experience of hand sawing is therefore an experience of using a dull tool badly, and they conclude, reasonably enough, that hand saws do not work. A properly sharpened saw of the right pattern cuts with surprisingly little effort, and the difference between a sharp saw and a dull one is not a matter of a few per cent but of several times the labour.

Cutting straight is a genuine skill, but it is a small and learnable one. It rests on four things, none of them mysterious: a saw that is sharp and evenly set, so it has no built-in tendency to curve; clear layout lines that tell the eye where the cut belongs; a body position that puts the arm, shoulder and eye in the plane of the cut so that the natural swing of the arm is already the right direction; and a stroke that is long, light and unhurried. Beginners typically fail on the last two, pushing hard with a short jabbing stroke and standing where they cannot see. Force is the enemy of accuracy in sawing more than in almost any other hand skill.

sections.heading: How a Saw Tooth Actually Cuts
sections.body:
A saw does not abrade wood; each tooth is a small cutting edge that removes a chip, and the whole blade is a gang of chisels or knives arranged in a row. Understanding the shape of one tooth explains almost every difference between saws.

Look at a saw edge from the side and each tooth is a triangle. The front face, leading in the cutting direction, is the cutting face; the back face is the relief; the curved valley between adjacent teeth is the gullet, which carries sawdust out of the cut. The gullet is not a decorative gap. Sawdust must be transported out of the kerf, and if the gullets fill, the saw stops cutting and starts rubbing. This is why coarse saws for thick wet timber have large gullets and fine saws for thin dry stock have small ones.

Three angles define the tooth. Rake is the tilt of the cutting face relative to a line square to the tooth line. Zero rake means the face is vertical, presenting the edge aggressively so it digs in and takes a big bite. Positive or relaxed rake, where the face leans back by 8, 15 or even 20 degrees, makes the tooth slice more gently, cut more slowly, and start far more easily without grabbing. Fleam is the angle at which the tooth is filed across the blade rather than square to it, which turns a chisel edge into a knife point. Set is the amount each tooth is bent sideways out of the plane of the plate.

The cutting action depends on grain direction, and this is the central fact of sawing. Wood is a bundle of long hollow cells, like a tight handful of drinking straws running along the length of the board. Cutting along that direction, called ripping, means splitting the straws lengthways, which a chisel edge does efficiently: a rip tooth filed with no fleam presents a tiny chisel that pares a shaving from the bottom of the kerf. Cutting across the direction, called crosscutting, means severing the straws, and a chisel pushed across them tears rather than cuts, leaving a ragged edge. A crosscut tooth is therefore filed with fleam so that its leading corner is a sharp point that scores the fibres like a knife before the rest of the tooth lifts out the waste between the two score lines.

The consequence is a rule with no exceptions worth worrying about: a rip saw dragged across the grain gives a rough, splintered, hard-going cut, while a crosscut saw used along the grain cuts slowly and inefficiently but does no harm. Using the wrong saw is not dangerous; it is simply worse.

sections.heading: Rip and Crosscut Filing in Detail
sections.body:
The distinction between rip and crosscut filing is what a saw sharpener actually controls, and knowing the numbers makes buying and sharpening intelligible rather than mystical.

A rip tooth is filed straight across the blade, with the file held at 90 degrees to the plate, so the tooth has a flat top edge running the full thickness of the steel, exactly like a tiny chisel. Rake is typically between 0 and 8 degrees for a saw meant to cut fast in softwood, and relaxed to 8 or 12 degrees for hardwood or for a saw a beginner will use, since aggressive zero-rake teeth catch and judder at the start of a cut. The action is that each tooth pares a shaving from the end grain at the bottom of the kerf, and the shavings produced are recognisably small shavings rather than dust. Because every tooth is doing the same paring, a rip saw removes material very quickly along the grain, and a 5 point rip saw in softwood will out-cut anything else moved by hand.

A crosscut tooth is filed with the file swung to an angle, the fleam, usually between 15 and 25 degrees, and alternate teeth are filed from opposite sides so the points lean in alternating directions. The result is a row of knife points, half of them scoring the left wall of the kerf and half the right. Each point severs the wood fibres cleanly at the surface, and the material between the two scored lines is crumbled out and carried away as dust. Rake on a crosscut saw is more relaxed, commonly 15 degrees, because the knife action does not need an aggressive bite and a relaxed tooth tracks a line more calmly. The waste from a crosscut saw is powdery, not shavings, which is a quick way to confirm what you are holding.

A hybrid filing sits between the two. Filing at zero fleam but with a relaxed rake of around 12 to 15 degrees produces a saw that rips well and crosscuts acceptably, and many people find one such saw more useful than owning two. Some sharpeners add a very small fleam of 5 to 10 degrees to a rip filing for the same reason.

Identifying an unknown saw takes ten seconds. Hold it so light rakes along the tooth line and look at the tops of the teeth. If the flats on top run square across the blade, it is rip filed. If the teeth come to alternating points leaning left and right, like a row of tiny spearheads, it is crosscut. If you are unsure, cut a scrap: shavings mean rip, dust means crosscut. Most cheap modern hardpoint saws are filed in a third pattern altogether, with three-sided teeth ground rather than filed on a machine, which cut both ways adequately, cannot be resharpened, and leave a coarse surface.

sections.heading: Set, Kerf and Why the Blade Does Not Jam
sections.body:
If the teeth of a saw lay exactly in the plane of the steel, the slot they cut would be the same width as the plate, and the plate would grip in it like a knife stuck in a log. Every saw therefore needs clearance, and there are two ways of providing it.

The usual method is set: alternate teeth are bent very slightly sideways, one to the left, the next to the right, so that the swath they sweep is wider than the body of the saw. The slot produced is the kerf, and its width is what the sawyer must account for when marking out. A sensible amount of set makes the kerf roughly one and a half times the plate thickness, which means each tooth is displaced by about a quarter of the plate thickness. Expressed differently, a panel saw with a plate of 0.9 millimetres wants a kerf of about 1.3 to 1.4 millimetres, while a fine dovetail saw with a plate of 0.5 millimetres may have a kerf barely 0.6 millimetres wide and set so slight it is hard to see.

More set is not better. Excess set makes the saw harder to push, because it removes more wood; makes it noisy and jumpy; leaves a rougher wall on the cut; and makes the saw wander, because a wide kerf gives the plate room to lean. Too little set makes the saw bind, heat up and stick, particularly in green, resinous or damp timber, which swells and closes on the blade. The correct amount depends on the wood: rough wet softwood needs generous set, dry hardwood and thin dry boards need very little, and a saw set for one is unpleasant in the other.

The second method of clearance is the taper grind, and better Western saws have both. The plate is ground thinner along the back than at the tooth line, sometimes also thinner toward the tip, so that once the teeth have cut a kerf the body of the blade sits in a slot already wider than itself. A well-tapered saw needs correspondingly less set, and therefore cuts more finely and easily. Some fine backsaws and most flush-cutting saws have no set at all and rely entirely on a thin plate; a flush-cut saw must have zero set on at least one face or it would score the surface it is trimming against.

Three practical consequences follow. First, always cut on the waste side of the line, because the kerf consumes material and a cut centred on the line makes the piece short by half a kerf. Second, a saw that pulls consistently to one side almost always has more set on that side, which is a repair rather than a technique problem. Third, if a saw binds mid-cut, the answer is a wedge in the kerf or better support of the workpiece, never more force.

sections.heading: Tooth Pitch: Points Per Inch and What to Choose
sections.body:
Tooth size is quoted in Western practice as points per inch, abbreviated ppi, counted by laying a rule on the tooth line and counting the points in one inch including both end points. Teeth per inch, tpi, counts the gaps instead, so ppi is always tpi plus one; an 8 point saw has 7 teeth per inch. Japanese saws and hacksaw blades are normally quoted in tpi. The difference matters when comparing catalogue figures and almost never otherwise.

The trade-off is straightforward. Coarse teeth, meaning few points per inch, have large gullets, remove a lot of wood per stroke, clear sawdust well and cut fast, but leave a rough surface and are hard to start. Fine teeth cut slowly, leave a smooth surface, start easily and follow a line more obediently, but clog in deep or damp cuts. The correct pitch is the coarsest that gives an acceptable finish for the job.

A rough set of working numbers covers most work. Full-size rip saws for breaking down boards along the grain run 4½ to 7 ppi. Full-size crosscut handsaws run 7 to 10 ppi. Panel saws, shorter at 20 to 22 inches for finer or thinner work, run 10 to 12 ppi. Tenon saws, backed and used for joint cheeks, run 12 to 14 ppi. Carcass saws for fine crosscutting run 13 to 15 ppi. Dovetail saws run 15 to 20 ppi, and very fine ones for small work go to 22. Hacksaws for metal run 14 to 32 tpi. Coping saw blades run 15 to 17 tpi.

Alongside pitch there is a rule that decides safety and smoothness in every material: at least three teeth must be in contact with the work at all times, and more is better. Fewer than three and the workpiece drops between teeth, the saw snatches, the cut chatters and, in metal, teeth break. This is why cutting thin sheet steel or a 1 millimetre wall tube demands a 32 tpi hacksaw blade and why using a 5 point rip saw on a thin plywood panel produces splintered chaos. In practice, count teeth against the thinnest section the saw will pass through, not the thickest.

Material matters as well as thickness. Plywood and MDF blunt saws quickly because of the glue, and their surfaces splinter, so a fine crosscut pitch of 10 to 12 ppi cutting with the good face upward on a Western saw, or downward on a pull saw, gives the cleanest result. Green or resinous softwood loads gullets, so go coarser than you would in dry timber and expect to clean the blade with paraffin or a solvent afterwards. A thin smear of candle wax or camellia oil along both faces of the plate reduces friction noticeably and slows rusting, and costs nothing.

sections.heading: The Western Panel Saw and Full-Size Handsaw
sections.body:
The unbacked handsaw is the general-purpose Western pattern: a tapering steel plate, wide at the heel where it meets the handle and narrow at the toe, with a closed pistol-grip handle usually of beech or apple. Because there is no stiffening back, the depth of cut is unlimited, which is what makes it the tool for sawing across a wide board or ripping a plank down its length.

Length is the first variable. The traditional full-size handsaw is 26 inches, occasionally 28, and the length is not for reach but for stroke economy: a long blade lets you use a long slow stroke that engages many teeth and stays straight. A panel saw is the same tool shortened to 20 or 22 inches, so named because it fits in a tool chest panel, and it is easier to control, easier to carry and better for sheet goods and finer stock. If you own one unbacked saw, a 22 inch panel saw at 10 ppi crosscut is the most generally useful choice.

The plate is normally spring steel hardened to around 50 to 52 on the Rockwell C scale, which is a deliberate compromise: hard enough to hold an edge for a reasonable time, soft enough that a triangular saw file will cut it. This is precisely the property the modern hardpoint saw discards, since its induction-hardened teeth are far harder, hold their edge several times longer and cannot be touched by a file. A hardpoint saw is a consumable; a traditional saw is a tool you maintain.

The handle deserves more attention than it usually gets, because it is what aims the saw. The hang, meaning the angle at which the grip sits relative to the tooth line, determines the direction in which your push is delivered. A low hang, with the grip more nearly in line with the teeth, drives the saw forward along the cut and suits ripping. A higher hang directs more of the push downward and suits crosscutting, where the saw must be encouraged into the fibres. A handle that fits, with the horns clear of the hand and the grip filling the palm, lets you hold the saw lightly, and a light grip is a straight cut; a clenched fist twists the plate.

Good second-hand saws by makers such as Disston, Spear and Jackson, Tyzack and Simonds are widely available for very little, since most people cannot sharpen them. A plate that is straight when sighted along the back, free of deep pitting at the tooth line and not kinked, is worth restoring almost regardless of how blunt or rusty it looks. Surface rust comes off with fine abrasive paper and oil, a loose handle is cured by tightening the split-nut screws, and blunt teeth are a filing job of perhaps twenty minutes.

sections.heading: Backsaws: Tenon, Carcass and Dovetail
sections.body:
A backsaw has a folded strip of brass or steel crimped over the top edge of the plate. That spine does two jobs. It stiffens a very thin plate so it cannot buckle, which allows the blade to be far thinner than an unbacked saw and therefore to cut a narrower kerf with less set and less effort. It also adds weight exactly where it is useful, above the cut, so the saw's own mass provides the downward pressure and the hand merely guides. The cost is that depth of cut is limited to the distance from tooth line to spine, typically 65 to 100 millimetres, so a backsaw cannot cut through anything deeper than that.

Backsaws are the joinery saws, and there are three common sizes. The tenon saw is the largest, with a plate 12 to 16 inches long and about 12 to 14 ppi, traditionally rip filed because its main job is sawing the cheeks of a tenon, which is a cut along the grain. The carcass saw is smaller, 10 to 12 inches, filed crosscut at 13 to 15 ppi, and is used for cutting shoulders and small components to length. The dovetail saw is smallest, 8 to 10 inches, 15 to 20 ppi, rip filed with a relaxed rake, with an open handle or a straight turned handle, and is used for the tails and pins of dovetails and for any fine cut along the grain.

The rip filing on dovetail and tenon saws surprises people who expect a fine saw to be crosscut, but joinery cuts run mostly along the grain, and a rip-filed saw leaves a cleaner wall in that direction and cuts noticeably faster. A rip-filed dovetail saw will still crosscut small stock acceptably because at 18 ppi each tooth removes very little.

Because backsaws are thin, light and low-set, they are the easiest saws with which to learn accuracy, and they are also the least forgiving of a heavy hand. The correct technique is to let the saw hang from the fingers, apply no downward pressure whatsoever, and move it. If a backsaw needs pushing down, it is blunt.

A related pattern is the mitre saw, essentially an oversized tenon saw of 20 to 30 inches used in a mitre box or a purpose-built frame that holds the blade at a set angle. A simple wooden mitre box with 45 and 90 degree slots, made in an hour from scrap, is one of the most useful accuracy aids available to someone who has not yet learnt to saw square by eye, and remains useful afterwards for repetitive work such as cutting a run of picture moulding or skirting returns.

sections.heading: Japanese Pull Saws
sections.body:
Japanese saws cut on the pull stroke rather than the push, and that single reversal changes everything about how the tool can be built. A blade under tension cannot buckle, so it does not need to resist compression, so it can be made very thin. Typical Japanese plates run 0.3 to 0.6 millimetres against 0.7 to 1.0 for a Western saw, and the kerf is correspondingly narrow, often under 0.5 millimetres for a fine dozuki. Less material removed means less effort, so a pull saw feels startlingly easy the first time it is used. The steel is also harder, commonly 60 to 65 Rockwell C against 50 to 52 in the West, which holds an edge much longer.

The three patterns worth knowing are simple. The ryoba is double-edged, with rip teeth along one edge and crosscut along the other, and no back, so it is the general-purpose saw and the one to buy first. The dozuki has a stiffening spine like a Western backsaw and very fine teeth, usually 18 to 25 tpi, and is the joinery saw for dovetails and shoulders. The kataba has a single toothed edge and no spine, so it cuts to unlimited depth with a fine tooth, useful for deep flush work and for cutting sheet goods.

The teeth themselves differ from Western practice. Japanese crosscut teeth are ground in three bevels rather than filed in two, giving a sharper point that severs fibres exceptionally cleanly, which is why a pull saw leaves a smoother surface than most Western saws. Most modern blades are impulse-hardened, recognisable by the dark grey or blackened teeth, and these cannot be resharpened; the blade unclips and is replaced for a fraction of the cost of the saw. Traditional non-hardened blades can be sharpened but require Japanese feather files and considerable skill.

The practical differences in use are worth rehearsing. Pull sawing puts the effort on the pull, so stance reverses: brace and draw, do not lean and shove. Because the blade is thin and hard it is brittle, and any sideways twist or attempt to lever the cut open will kink or snap it; a broken Japanese blade is almost always a twisted one. Start the cut with the far end of the blade at a very shallow angle and almost no pressure. And because the good face should be up on a Western saw but down on a pull saw, sheet goods must be turned over relative to habit if the visible face is to stay free of breakout.

Neither tradition is simply better. Pull saws cut faster and finer with less skill; Western saws are more robust, resharpenable indefinitely, and better in rough, dirty or awkward work.

sections.heading: Specialist Saws and What Each Is For
sections.body:
Beyond the general patterns sits a family of saws each designed around a shape of cut the others cannot make, and knowing which one to reach for saves a great deal of struggling.

The coping saw holds a thin replaceable blade about 165 millimetres long under tension in a sprung steel frame with a throat of roughly 120 millimetres. Its blade can be rotated in its pins so the frame clears the work, which makes it the tool for cutting curves and for removing waste between dovetail pins. Blades are 15 to 17 tpi and, in the usual convention, are mounted teeth pointing toward the handle so the saw cuts on the pull, which keeps the fine blade in tension and stops it wandering. The fret saw is its finer cousin, with a much deeper throat of 300 millimetres or more and very fine blades, for delicate interior curves in thin stock.

The bow saw or frame saw stretches a narrow blade between two arms tensioned by a twisted cord and toggle. Because the blade is tensioned rather than stiffened by its own width, it can be narrow enough to turn a curve while long enough to cut deeply, and the large versions were the primary tool for converting logs before machinery. A modern equivalent is the tubular-frame bow saw for green wood and firewood, with coarse raker-pattern teeth designed to clear wet fibrous sawdust.

The keyhole, compass or pad saw is a narrow tapering blade with no frame at all, allowing it to be started in a drilled hole and steered around an interior cut. Its close relative the drywall or jab saw has a hardened point that can be punched straight through plasterboard, and coarse teeth that survive gypsum, which is abrasive enough to destroy a woodworking saw.

The flush-cut saw has a very thin flexible plate with no set on at least one face, so it can be laid flat against a surface to trim a protruding dowel or peg without scoring the wood around it. The veneer saw has a small curved toothed edge for scoring across thin sheet.

For metal, the hacksaw holds a blade under high tension in a rigid frame. Blades are 300 millimetres between pin centres in the common size, and pitch runs 14 tpi for thick soft metals, 18 for general work, 24 for thinner sections and 32 for thin-wall tube and sheet, chosen so at least three teeth are always in contact. Blades are fitted teeth forward and cut on the push. Pruning saws, finally, use coarse widely-set impulse-hardened teeth on a curved blade cutting on the pull, because green wood is wet, fibrous and clogs anything finer.

sections.heading: Choosing a Saw and Assembling a Working Kit
sections.body:
Almost nobody needs the full historical range. Three saws cover the overwhelming majority of domestic and workshop cutting, and a fourth adds curves. Spending the available money on fewer, better saws is far more useful than buying a set, because a sharp mid-priced saw outperforms an expensive dull one and every saw in a bargain set is dull.

When buying new, the decision is essentially between a resharpenable Western saw, a hardpoint Western saw and a Japanese saw with replaceable blades. A hardpoint is the right answer for site work, reclaimed timber containing hidden nails, and anything abrasive, because it will not be sharpened anyway and losing it costs little. A resharpenable saw is right for anyone willing to spend an hour learning to file, since it will then outlast its owner. A Japanese saw is the fastest route to clean accurate cuts for a beginner, at the cost of fragility and of blades that must be bought rather than restored.

When buying second-hand, the checks are quick. Sight along the back of the plate for straightness; a gentle bow is correctable, a sharp kink is not. Flex the plate a little and let it spring back true. Look for deep pitting at the tooth line, which is fatal since sharpening cannot remove it, whereas rust and pitting on the flat of the plate is only cosmetic. Check that the handle is not cracked through the horns and that the fixing screws are present. Blunt teeth, missing teeth and uneven set are all repairable.
ingredients: A 20 to 22 inch panel saw, 10 points per inch, crosscut filed, for cutting boards and sheet goods to length; the single most useful saw to own.
A rip saw or hybrid-filed saw of 5 to 7 points per inch, or a Japanese ryoba, for cutting along the grain.
A 10 inch dovetail or carcass backsaw, 15 to 18 points per inch, for joints and any cut where the surface will be seen.
A coping saw with a dozen spare 15 tpi blades, for curves and for clearing dovetail waste.
A hacksaw frame with 18, 24 and 32 tpi blades if any metal, bolt or tube will ever be cut.
A try square or combination square with a true 90 degree blade, checked by drawing a line, flipping the square and drawing again: the two lines must coincide.
A marking knife or a sharp craft knife, plus a hard pencil of 2H or harder sharpened to a chisel point.
A marking gauge for lines parallel to an edge, and a sliding bevel for angles other than square.
Two sawhorses or a bench with a vice, so the work can be held still at a workable height.
A triangular saw file of the right size, a saw set and a mill file, if the saws are to be maintained rather than replaced.
Safety glasses, and a dust mask when cutting MDF, plywood or plasterboard.

sections.heading: Marking Out: The Layout That Makes a Straight Cut Possible
sections.body:
No amount of sawing skill rescues bad layout. A cut can only be as accurate as the line it follows, and most cuts that end up crooked were doomed before the saw touched the wood.

Start from a reference. Choose one face and one edge of the board, confirm they are flat and square to each other, and mark them, traditionally with a looping face mark and a caret on the edge pointing to it. Every measurement and every square line then comes from those two surfaces. Measuring from a rough or out-of-square edge guarantees compounding error, and measuring each cut from the end of the previous one accumulates it; wherever possible take all measurements from a single datum.

Use a knife rather than a pencil for any cut that must be accurate. A pencil line is 0.5 millimetres wide at best and sits on top of the fibres; a knife line is a severed groove perhaps 0.1 millimetres wide, and it does two extra jobs. It cuts the surface fibres so they cannot tear out as the saw enters, giving a cleaner edge, and it leaves a physical wall that a chisel or the saw plate can be dropped into, so the tool locates itself by feel. The standard refinement is to deepen the knife line on the waste side into a shallow V-shaped trench with a chisel, creating a positive shoulder for the saw to sit against.

Square the line right around the workpiece, not just across the face. A line on the face tells you where to start; a line down the near edge tells you whether the cut is staying vertical; a line on the far face tells you where to finish. Sawing to two visible lines simultaneously is what produces a cut that is square in both planes, and it is far easier than trying to hold a blade vertical by feel.

Mark the waste side unmistakably, with hatching or a large X. This sounds trivial and prevents a large fraction of ruined workpieces, because under concentration it is remarkably easy to saw on the wrong side of the line and lose a kerf width of material from the part you wanted. Then cut so the kerf falls entirely in the waste, with the teeth just kissing the line and leaving it intact on the finished piece, a practice usually described as leaving the line. If the fit must be exact, leave the line and pare down to it with a plane or chisel, since removing a shaving is easy and putting one back is not.

One further habit repays itself constantly: when several identical pieces are needed, do not measure each one. Cut the first, check it, then use it as a template against which the rest are marked, or clamp a stop block to a fence and butt each piece against it. Repeated measuring introduces a fresh chance of error every time, whereas a physical stop reproduces the same length indefinitely.

sections.heading: Stance, Grip and Starting the Cut
sections.body:
The mechanics of a straight cut are mostly settled before the first full stroke. A saw is guided by the swing of the whole arm, and the arm swings in a plane fixed by where the body stands. If that plane matches the intended cut, straightness is nearly automatic; if it does not, the wrist must correct continuously and the cut will wander.

Set the work at a height that lets the arm swing freely: roughly knee height for crosscutting on sawhorses, hip to waist height for a backsaw at a bench. Too high is the commoner error, and it forces the elbow out sideways, which curves the cut.

Hold the saw lightly, with the index finger extended along the side of the handle pointing where the cut is going. That finger reduces the tendency to clench and aligns the hand with the plate. Position the body so shoulder, elbow, wrist and plate lie in one vertical plane containing the cut line, with the eye above it. Standing to one side is the commonest cause of a leaning cut.

Two aids help judge vertical: a small square stood beside the blade, and, on a clean bright plate, the reflection trick. When the saw is square, the reflection of the board appears to continue the board itself without a step; a leaning saw shows a visible kink.
steps: Clamp or otherwise secure the work so it cannot move, and support it so the offcut will not sag and pinch the kerf closed near the end of the cut.
Position yourself so that the shoulder, elbow and saw lie in the plane of the cut line, with your eye above it, and check that the arm can swing its full travel without meeting your body.

Place the saw at the far edge of the work, on the waste side of the line, using the knuckle of the thumb of your other hand raised vertically against the plate as a fence, keeping the thumb well clear of the teeth.
Lift the saw so only the last few teeth touch, hold the blade at a shallow angle of about 20 degrees, and make two or three short backward strokes with no downward pressure to nick a starting groove.

Once the groove is deep enough to hold the blade, move the guiding hand away and begin light forward strokes, gradually raising the saw to its working angle: about 45 degrees for crosscutting, 60 degrees for ripping, and as low as 20 degrees for a fine backsaw or a pull saw.
Lengthen the stroke until you are using almost the whole blade, counting perhaps one stroke a second, and let the weight of the saw supply all the downward force.
Watch the line ahead of the teeth rather than the teeth themselves, exactly as a driver watches the road ahead rather than the bonnet, and check the near edge line every few strokes for squareness.
Approach the end of the cut by shortening the stroke and slowing, supporting the offcut with the free hand so it cannot break away and tear a splinter from the underside.

sections.heading: Sawing to the Line and Steering a Cut Back
sections.body:
Once the cut is established, the whole task becomes maintaining a line already begun, and the governing principle is that a saw is steered gently over many strokes rather than corrected in one.

Use the full length of the blade. A short jabbing stroke of 100 millimetres uses a handful of teeth, wears that patch of the saw unevenly, generates heat and gives the plate no chance to settle into the kerf. A long stroke of 300 to 500 millimetres on a full-size saw distributes wear, clears the gullets properly, and is markedly less tiring because the arm moves at a lower force for longer. Count roughly one complete stroke per second and resist speeding up; speed comes from stroke length, not cadence.

Apply essentially no downward pressure. A sharp saw of any pattern cuts under its own weight, and on the return stroke the pressure should be released entirely so the teeth skim back rather than dragging. Pushing down does not cut faster, it makes the plate flex, and a flexed plate cuts a curve.

When the cut begins to drift, the wrong response is to lever the saw sideways, which twists the plate, jams it and can kink a thin blade permanently. The right response is to twist the handle a few degrees so the teeth are aimed very slightly back toward the line, then take a series of light strokes with the saw riding mostly on the back of the kerf, allowing the teeth to shave the near wall over 10 or 20 strokes until the cut has walked back. It is slow and it is invisible to a watcher, and it works. If the drift is severe, the cleanest remedy is often to stop, start a fresh kerf from the correct line at the far end and meet the old cut.

For a cut that must be square in both planes, keep two lines in view and favour whichever is going wrong. On a wide board, cut the near corner down first at a steep angle so a shallow kerf runs across the face, then lower the saw and let that kerf act as a guide while the cut deepens; the established groove will hold the plate.

For ripping a long board, the kerf tends to close behind the saw as internal stresses release, gripping the plate. Drive a thin wedge or a screwdriver into the kerf a foot behind the teeth to hold it open, and move it along as you progress. For sheet goods, support the panel across its width on battens so it cannot flex, keep the good face upward with a Western saw and downward with a Japanese one, and score the cut line with a knife first to prevent surface breakout.

sections.heading: Sharpening: Jointing, Shaping, Setting and Filing
sections.body:
Sharpening a saw is a genuine craft skill, but the basic operation is within reach of anyone who can file steel, and it transforms a tool. Only saws with unhardened teeth, bright rather than blackened, can be sharpened; a hardpoint or impulse-hardened blade will simply skate a file across its surface.

The equipment is modest: a triangular saw file of the correct size, a flat mill file, a saw set, and a way of holding the plate rigidly along its tooth line, which is what a saw vice does and which two pieces of hardwood clamped in a bench vice do nearly as well. File size follows tooth pitch, since the file must be large enough that only its lower third is used: a regular taper for 4 to 6 ppi, slim for 7 to 10, extra slim for 11 to 14, and double extra slim for 15 ppi and finer.

The sequence has four stages, always in the same order. Jointing comes first: run a flat mill file along the tooth line, held square, until a small flat appears on the tip of every tooth. This is deliberately blunting the saw, and it is the step beginners skip. Its purpose is to establish that all teeth are exactly the same height, because a single tall tooth does all the work, snatches, and makes the saw impossible to start. The flats also become the visual gauge for the filing that follows.

Shaping restores the tooth profile. Working with the triangular file held horizontal and at the chosen rake angle, file each gullet until the flats left by jointing are reduced to roughly half their size, keeping every tooth the same size and spacing. Setting comes next, using a saw set, a plier-like tool with an adjustable anvil that bends the top third of a tooth outward by a controlled amount. Set every other tooth from one side, then reverse the saw and set the alternate teeth from the other. Set only the upper portion; bending a tooth at its root will crack it.

Sharpening is the final pass. For rip filing, hold the file square across the plate and take the same number of strokes in every gullet, working along the saw and finishing when the flats have just disappeared. For crosscut, swing the file to the fleam angle, file every second gullet from the handle end, then turn the saw around and file the remaining gullets from the other side. Consistency matters more than perfect angles: a saw filed slightly wrong but identically all along will cut straight, while a saw filed perfectly in places and unevenly elsewhere will not.

sections.heading: Diagnosing a Cut That Went Wrong
sections.body:
Almost every bad cut has a small number of possible causes, and the shape of the failure identifies which.

A cut that leans consistently to one side, angling away from vertical, is usually the sawyer rather than the saw. The body is standing out of the plane of the cut, or the eye is off to one side, or the elbow is being held away from the body because the work is too high. The test is to have the same cut made by someone else with the same saw; if their cut is square, the tool is fine. If both cuts lean the same way, the saw has more set on one side, or its teeth are duller on one side, and it needs jointing, resetting and refiling.

A cut that starts square and curves progressively is usually a bowed or flexing plate caused by pressing down, or a kerf being levered by attempts to steer. It can also be caused by following grain: a saw pushed hard along the grain will follow a hard growth ring in preference to your line, exactly as a chisel follows the grain. The remedy is less pressure, a longer stroke and cutting slightly to the waste side so there is material to plane back to.

A saw that binds and stops has lost clearance. The kerf has closed because the workpiece is unsupported and sagging, because internal stress has released as the board is ripped, or because the wood is damp or resinous and swelling onto the plate. Wedge the kerf open, support the offcut, and if it recurs the saw needs more set for that material. Heat and a squealing noise are the early warning.

A saw that will not start, skittering across the surface and jumping out of position, has aggressive rake, a tall tooth left by poor jointing, or is simply being pushed rather than drawn. Start on the backstroke, hold it at a shallow angle, use no pressure, and guide it with a raised thumb knuckle or a scrap block clamped along the line.

Ragged, splintered edges mean the wrong filing or the wrong pitch: a rip saw used across the grain, too coarse a tooth for the thickness, or a blunt saw tearing rather than severing. Score the line with a knife, use a finer pitch, and support the underside with a sacrificial board so the fibres at the exit have something to press against.

Finally, a cut that is accurate but in the wrong place is a layout failure, not a sawing one, and the fix is always upstream: work from one datum, mark the waste, and cut on the waste side of the line.

sections.heading: Care, Storage and Building the Skill
sections.body:
A saw is a spring-steel blade with a fine edge, and both are easily spoiled by neglect. Rust is the chief enemy, since pitting at the tooth line is unrepairable, and steel rusts fastest where a bare hand has touched it, because sweat is salty and acidic. Wipe the plate after use and put a thin film of oil, paste wax or camellia oil on it; a rag kept lightly oiled in a jar and drawn over the blade takes two seconds. Store saws hanging by the handle or in slotted racks so nothing rests on the teeth, and if they must be carried loose, split a length of garden hose lengthways and press it over the tooth line as a guard.

Sharpness lasts far longer if the saw never meets anything harder than wood. Nails, screws, staples, grit embedded in reclaimed timber and the abrasive fillers in MDF and plasterboard will all take the edge off in seconds. Reclaimed timber deserves a magnet and a careful inspection before cutting, and a cheap hardpoint saw kept for dirty work protects the good ones. Cutting into a bench top or a concrete floor at the end of a stroke does more damage than a month of ordinary use, so put a sacrificial board underneath.

Learning to cut straight is a matter of a few hours of deliberate practice, not years. The most efficient exercise is unglamorous: take a length of scrap softwood, square a line right around it, and cut it off. Then check the cut with a square in both planes, note which way it is out, and cut again 20 millimetres along. Twenty cuts in a session and a note of the error each time teaches the body more than any amount of reading, because the correction is applied while the memory of the stroke is fresh.

Two refinements accelerate it. First, practise starting, since the first five strokes determine the cut and most errors are established there; make fifty starts without completing any of them. Second, practise sawing to a line rather than sawing off a board, by marking a line down the face of a wide piece and cutting along it for 200 millimetres, which exposes drift far more clearly than a short crosscut.

Expect to reach acceptable accuracy, within perhaps half a millimetre over the width of a board, within a few sessions, and to keep improving slowly for years. A hand saw rewards patience in a way few tools do: the technique is not difficult, but it cannot be hurried, and every attempt to force it makes the result worse. The commonest mistake among people who have been sawing badly for years is simply gripping too hard and pushing too fast, and the commonest surprise, once that is corrected, is how little effort a sharp saw actually needs.

guides.safetyNote: Keep the guiding thumb raised on its knuckle and well clear of the tooth line when starting a cut; a saw that jumps out of its groove travels toward the hand steadying the work. Always secure the workpiece so it cannot shift, and support the offcut at the end of a cut so it cannot fall or twist the blade. Wear safety glasses, and a dust mask when cutting MDF, plywood or plasterboard, whose dust is a respiratory irritant and, in the case of hardwood and MDF dust, a recognised carcinogen with long-term exposure. Never attempt to free a jammed blade by levering it sideways: a thin hardened plate, particularly a Japanese one, can snap and throw fragments. Check reclaimed timber for nails and screws with a magnet before cutting.

guides.title: Circular Saw Setup and Safe Technique
guides.summary: How a circular saw works and how to use one well: choosing and mounting blades, setting depth and bevel, supporting the work, understanding and preventing kickback, making accurate crosscuts and rips, and maintaining the tool.

sections.heading: What a Circular Saw Is and Why Technique Matters
sections.body: A circular saw is a handheld motor spinning a toothed disc at somewhere between 4,000 and 6,000 revolutions per minute — at the rim of a standard 7¼-inch (184 mm) blade, the teeth are traveling at roughly 120 miles per hour, about 55 meters per second. It is the tool that breaks down sheet goods, crosscuts framing lumber, trims doors, and builds decks; for most home workshops it is the first and most-used power saw, capable of doing perhaps 80 percent of what a table saw does at a tenth of the cost and weight. It is also, together with the table saw, responsible for a large share of the tens of thousands of saw-related emergency room visits recorded every year in the United States alone — lacerations and amputations of fingers and hands above all, but also thigh injuries from saws set down while still spinning and eye injuries from thrown debris. Here is the fact that reframes everything: the majority of circular saw accidents are not caused by a hand wandering into a blade in plain view. They are caused by kickback — the saw binding in the cut and hurling itself backward toward the operator faster than any human reflex can respond — and by its cousins: the blade grabbing an unsupported offcut, the guard failing to close, the cut pinching shut. These are physics events, not attention lapses, and they are almost entirely preventable by setup: how the work is supported, how deep the blade is set, where the operator's body is, and whether the saw is allowed to cut in a straight, unpinched line. That is why this guide spends as much space on preparing a cut as on making one. Technique matters for quality, too, and the same habits serve both masters. A saw guided smoothly along a straight reference, with a sharp blade at the correct depth through well-supported material, cuts safely and leaves a clean, square edge; a saw forced freehand through pinching wood with a dull blade wanders, burns, splinters the veneer, and stalls — and every one of those quality failures is simultaneously a safety hazard. Learning the circular saw is therefore not a matter of courage but of understanding perhaps a dozen mechanisms: why the blade cuts upward through the material, why the motor twists the saw when teeth jam, why an offcut must be free to fall, why depth of cut controls how violently the saw can react. This guide works through the machine itself — motor styles, base, guards, adjustments — then blade selection and mounting, the geometry of supporting work correctly, kickback in detail, the standard cuts from crosscut to plunge, protective equipment, and finally maintenance and what to do when a cut goes wrong mid-stroke. A reader who absorbs the mechanisms will find the rules obvious, because every rule in circular saw work is just a mechanism read backward.

sections.heading: Anatomy of the Saw: Sidewinders, Worm Drives, and the Parts That Matter
sections.body: Circular saws come in two mechanical families, and knowing both explains most of what you see in a tool aisle. The sidewinder, or direct-drive saw, mounts the blade on the motor's own shaft, spinning it fast — typically 5,000 to 6,000 rpm. It is compact, relatively light at 8 to 10 pounds, and on most models the blade sits on the right side of the motor. The worm drive places the motor behind the blade, driving it through a pair of gears that trade speed for torque: the blade turns slower, around 4,300 rpm, but with substantially more twisting force, which is why framers cutting wet lumber and stacked sheets have favored worm drives for generations. They are longer, heavier — 13 to 16 pounds — and traditionally carry the blade on the left, giving a right-handed user a clear view of the cut line. Cordless saws, now genuinely capable on 18-volt and 36-volt platforms, are almost all sidewinder layouts, many with the blade on the left. None of these choices changes safety fundamentals; they change balance, sightlines, and stamina. The parts that matter operationally are the same on every saw. The shoe, or base plate, is the flat sole the saw rides on; everything about cut quality depends on it staying flat on the work, and everything about accuracy depends on the blade being parallel to its edge. The upper guard is a fixed housing over the blade's top half. The lower guard is a spring-loaded shroud that covers the blade's exposed lower arc and retracts automatically as the leading edge of the work pushes it back during a cut, then snaps closed when the saw exits. It is the single most important safety device on the tool: a functioning lower guard is what lets you set a still-coasting saw down without it crawling across the workpiece or your leg. The depth-adjustment lever unlocks the shoe so it pivots away from the blade, controlling how much tooth projects below; the bevel adjustment tilts the shoe from 0 to typically 45 or 56 degrees for angled cuts. At the front of the shoe are kerf notches — sighting marks, usually one for square cuts and one for 45-degree bevels, showing where the blade will actually cut. A spindle lock button freezes the arbor — the shaft the blade mounts on, ⅝ inch in diameter on standard saws — so the arbor nut can be loosened with the supplied wrench. The trigger often includes a safety interlock that must be depressed first, and better saws add an electric brake that stops the blade within about two seconds of trigger release rather than letting it freewheel for ten. Finally, note which way the blade spins: the teeth at the bottom of the blade move from the front of the saw toward the rear — the blade cuts upward through the material. That single fact determines which face of the work splinters, why the saw pulls itself forward slightly, and much of the kickback story.

sections.heading: Choosing a Blade: Teeth, Kerf, and Grind
sections.body: The blade does the cutting; the saw only spins it, and a $15 blade upgrade improves a cheap saw more than any other purchase. Start with diameter and bore: the overwhelming standard for full-size saws is 7¼ inches with a ⅝-inch arbor hole, giving a maximum depth of cut around 2½ inches at 90 degrees — enough to cut doubled framing lumber — while compact cordless saws use 6½-inch or smaller blades. Never mount a blade rated for a lower maximum rpm than the saw produces; the rating is printed on the plate, and modern carbide blades for 7¼-inch saws are generally rated 7,000 rpm or more, comfortably above any saw's speed. Tooth count sets the trade between speed and finish. Fewer teeth mean bigger gullets — the valleys between teeth that carry sawdust out — so the blade clears chips fast and cuts aggressively but leaves a rougher edge: 18 to 24 teeth is the framing standard for ripping and general construction. More teeth take smaller bites for a cleaner edge but cut slower and heat faster: 40 teeth is a good general-purpose and crosscut count, and 60 in a 7¼-inch blade is a finish or plywood blade. Nearly all modern blades carry carbide tips brazed to a steel plate; carbide holds an edge ten to twenty times longer than plain steel and survives the abrasive glues in plywood and MDF. Kerf — the width of the slot the blade cuts — matters more than beginners expect. A full-kerf blade cuts about ⅛ inch (3.2 mm) wide and has a stiff plate that resists deflection; a thin-kerf blade, around 3⁄32 inch (2.4 mm), removes roughly a quarter less wood, so it cuts noticeably faster and is easier on cordless batteries and low-powered saws, at the cost of a slightly whippier plate that can flex in dense stock. For a battery saw, thin kerf is almost always right. The grind — the shape sharpened onto each carbide tip — is the fine print worth reading. ATB, alternate top bevel, angles successive teeth left and right so they shear wood fibers cleanly; it is the standard for crosscutting and plywood. FTG, flat top grind, has square-topped teeth that chisel straight through — fast, durable rip blades. Combination blades group ATB teeth with a periodic flat raker to do both jobs acceptably. TCG, triple-chip grind, alternates a chamfered tooth with a flat one and is the choice for laminates, plastics, and non-ferrous metal with the right blade body. Specialty discs extend the saw's reach: abrasive discs and, far better, diamond blades cut masonry and tile (dusty, and dangerous silica dust at that — cut wet or with extraction); dedicated cold-cut carbide blades handle steel roofing in saws rated for metal. A practical kit for a homeowner is simply two blades: a 24-tooth thin-kerf framing blade for construction lumber, and a 40- to 60-tooth ATB blade reserved for plywood, trim, and anything with a face that shows.

sections.heading: Mounting a Blade Correctly
sections.body: Changing a blade is a two-minute job that people get wrong in three classic ways: blade backwards, saw still energized, and debris trapped between the blade and its washers. The energizing error is the dangerous one — a saw that starts while your fingers are wrapped around its blade is a life-changing event — so the rule is absolute: cord unplugged from the wall, or battery physically removed from the tool, before the wrench comes out. Not switched off; disconnected. The direction error is the most common. A circular saw blade must rotate so its teeth attack the material from below and travel upward through it at the front of the saw; every blade carries a printed arrow, and every saw has a matching arrow on the upper or lower guard. Teeth on a correctly mounted blade point forward and up at the bottom of the saw's front edge. A backwards blade will still cut, after a fashion — friction and the backs of the carbide tips burn through wood, smoking, dulling the blade, and dramatically raising the chance of a violent grab — which is exactly why the error goes unnoticed by beginners. The debris error is subtler: sawdust or a chip caught between the arbor flange washers and the blade plate tilts the blade minutely, producing wobble that widens the kerf and vibrates the arbor nut loose; wipe both washers and the blade's bore clean at every change. The mechanical sequence itself is short and nearly identical on every saw. Two details deserve emphasis: on most saws the arbor nut loosens in the direction the blade spins — the wrench pulls against rotation — so the nut self-tightens in use; check the manual rather than forcing anything. And tighten only snug plus a modest pull: the flange washers grip the blade, the spindle lock resists the torque, and overtightening merely makes the next change miserable.
steps: 1. Disconnect power completely: unplug the cord or remove the battery from the saw. Do not rely on the switch.
2. Set the saw on its side, press the spindle lock, and rotate the blade by hand until the arbor locks solid.
3. Loosen the arbor nut with the supplied wrench, pulling against the direction of blade rotation; remove nut and outer flange washer.
4. Hold the lower guard retracted, slide the old blade off the arbor, and remove it through the shoe opening.
5. Wipe the inner and outer flange washers, the arbor, and the new blade's bore clean of dust and resin.
6. Mount the new blade with its rotation arrow matching the arrow on the saw's guard — teeth pointing up and forward at the front of the saw.
7. Replace the outer washer and nut, thread by hand, then tighten snug with the wrench against the spindle lock. Do not overtighten.
8. Release the spindle lock, spin the blade by hand to check for wobble and scraping, and confirm the lower guard snaps fully shut on its own.
9. Stow the wrench, reconnect power, and make a short test cut in scrap before cutting real work.

sections.heading: Setting Depth of Cut and Bevel: Small Adjustments, Large Consequences
sections.body: Depth of cut is the most neglected adjustment on the tool and one of the most important safety settings you control. The rule: set the blade so its teeth clear the underside of the material by about ¼ inch — roughly one full tooth, gullet included, showing below the work. To set it, disconnect power, retract the lower guard, hold the shoe flat against the edge of the material, release the depth lever, pivot the base until the blade projects the right amount, and lock it firmly. The reasons are mechanical, and worth actually understanding because they motivate an unglamorous habit. First, exposure: every millimeter of blade hanging below the work is bare spinning steel with nothing but the lower guard between it and whatever lies beneath — sawhorse, cord, thigh. Second, kickback geometry: with a shallow setting, the tooth arc meets the wood at a steep, efficient shearing angle, and if the blade does bind, the small engaged arc gives the pinch less blade to grab. A blade buried three inches deep in one-inch stock presents a long, nearly vertical cutting arc; a pinch anywhere along it acts like a brake shoe clamped on a flywheel, and the saw's 5,000 rpm has to go somewhere — it goes into throwing the machine backward. Third, quality: correct depth minimizes splintering, because teeth exit the surface at a low angle rather than punching steeply through the face. There are exceptions — cutting into a surface where you must not mark what is behind it (sawing flooring over joists you want untouched, or scoring to a controlled partial depth for a dado-style trench), where the depth setting becomes a precision instrument: set it against a ruler or by holding the shoe on the work and measuring tooth projection. The bevel adjustment tilts the blade relative to the shoe, from 0 degrees (square) usually to 45 and often past it to 50-plus for roof work. Two things change when you tilt. The effective depth of cut shrinks — at 45 degrees a saw that cuts 2½ inches square manages only about 1¾ — and the lower guard becomes more prone to snagging on the work's edge at the start of the cut, so a beveled entry often needs the guard eased back manually by its lever for the first inch, then released. Never wedge or tie it open. Trust neither the depth scale nor the bevel scale on a new or dropped saw: check squareness by disconnecting power, retracting the guard, and holding a speed square or combination square against the shoe and the blade plate (between teeth, which are wider than the plate), adjusting the 0-degree stop screw until blade and base agree. Do the same check against a marked 45. A saw whose shoe is not square to its blade cannot cut a square edge no matter how carefully you guide it, and a beveled edge that should be square is the classic sign — doors that will not seat, joints that gap — of a bumped bevel lock nobody noticed.

sections.heading: Power: Cords, Amps, Batteries, and Circuits
sections.body: A full-size corded circular saw draws 12 to 15 amperes under load — essentially the entire capacity of a standard North American 15-amp branch circuit — and how you feed it electricity has real consequences for both the tool and you. Undersized extension cords are the classic mistake. A long, thin cord acts as a resistor: voltage sags at the saw, the motor draws more current to compensate, and both cord and motor heat. Chronic voltage starvation cooks motor windings and, in the short term, robs the saw of the torque that keeps it from stalling mid-cut — and a stalling saw is a binding, kick-prone saw. The working rule: for a 15-amp saw, use 12-gauge wire for cords up to 50 feet and 10-gauge beyond that, and treat 16-gauge household cords as unsuitable, period. Uncoil cords fully — a tightly coiled cord under load traps heat remarkably well — and route the cord over your shoulder or behind you during cuts, because sawing through your own cord is not a rare accident; it is one of the most common. It is also an argument for plugging into a GFCI-protected outlet or pigtail whenever you work outdoors or anywhere damp: the ground-fault interrupter trips in milliseconds at around 5 milliamps of leakage, well below the threshold of a dangerous shock. Inspect the cord and plug before each session; a nicked jacket near the saw's strain relief is a defect to repair, not to tape and forget. Cordless saws have rewritten the practical calculus. A modern brushless saw on a 5-amp-hour or larger battery genuinely rivals corded cutting performance for most tasks and eliminates cord hazards entirely, at the price of two new habits. First, battery discipline: a fading battery does not just cut slower — as voltage sags, torque falls, and users unconsciously push harder, which is precisely the recipe for a bind; swap to a charged pack when the saw starts laboring rather than leaning on it. Second, the removed battery is your lockout: pull it for every blade change and every adjustment, exactly as you would unplug a cord. Two behavioral points apply to both power types. Let the motor reach full speed before the blade touches wood — starting in contact with the work is a guaranteed lurch — and let the blade do the work at its own pace. Feed pressure should be firm and steady; if the motor note drops deeply and the cut slows, you are either feeding too fast, running a dull or wrong blade, or the kerf is pinching, and the correct response is to ease off and diagnose, not to shove. On the electrical-safety side, know your saw's class: most modern consumer saws are double-insulated (marked with a square-within-a-square symbol) and carry two-prong plugs by design; older metal-bodied saws rely on a grounding prong that must never be cut off or bypassed with an ungrounded adapter. If a saw trips breakers repeatedly, sparks visibly through its vents beyond the normal faint brush glow, smells of scorched varnish, or shocks you even faintly — retire it from service until repaired.

sections.heading: Supporting the Work: The Geometry That Prevents Most Accidents
sections.body: Before the trigger is ever pulled, the fate of a cut is largely decided by one question: what will the kerf — the slot the blade is cutting — do as the saw passes through? There are only two safe answers. Either the kerf stays open, or it opens wider as the offcut tips gently away. The catastrophic answer is that it closes and pinches the blade. This is the entire theory of workpiece support, and it is worth internalizing as geometry rather than as a list of rules. Consider a board supported at both ends, like a plank across two sawhorses, cut in the middle. As the blade severs the last fibers, both halves sag toward each other — supported only at their outer ends, they hinge downward at the cut — and the kerf clamps the blade like a vise. The saw, still spinning at full speed, is now seized by the work: it kicks. Now consider the same board supported so the cut falls just outside one support, with the offcut free: as the fibers part, the offcut drops away, the kerf opens, and the blade never feels a thing. That is the universal pattern: support the keeper side well, let the waste side fall. For short offcuts, simply letting them drop is correct; never hold them, and never have a helper hold them — a person supporting an offcut instinctively lifts it as it comes free, closing the kerf. For long or heavy offcuts that would splinter free before the cut completes or fall dangerously, support the work on four points arranged so that the two central supports flank the cut line closely — the classic arrangement on framing lumber — or, better for sheet goods, lay the entire panel on a sacrificial bed. The cheapest and best sheet-cutting bed is a slab of 1½- or 2-inch rigid foam insulation on the floor or across sawhorses: the panel is supported everywhere, both sides of the kerf lie dead still as the cut completes, the blade (set to that ¼-inch depth) harmlessly scores the foam, and you can kneel on the work itself. Strips of scrap lumber laid crosswise under a panel work too, if the blade path runs between or across them shallow enough to only nick them. Stability of the whole arrangement matters as much as kerf behavior: sawhorses on level ground, the work clamped when it is light enough that saw thrust could slide it — a small workpiece must always be clamped, never held with one hand while sawing with the other, because a saw exiting a cut travels exactly where your holding hand is. Check under the work before every cut: the protruding blade will find any cord, clamp bar, sawhorse stretcher, or concrete floor under the line. Finally, think about where the saw's weight rests as the cut ends. The shoe must remain fully supported on the keeper side until the blade exits; a saw whose base tips into the opening kerf at the end of a cut leaves a ragged edge and a moment of unguarded, misdirected blade.

sections.heading: Kickback: The Physics of the Saw's One Real Attack
sections.body: Kickback is what happens when the rotational energy of the blade is suddenly converted into linear motion of the saw, and understanding it mechanically is the single most valuable piece of knowledge in circular saw work. The blade spins toward the operator at its top — remember, teeth travel front-to-back over the top of the arc — so when the blade is seized by the work, the reaction flings the saw up and backward, toward the user, with the motor's full torque plus the flywheel energy of the blade behind it.
